title: System Design
description: Learn to design scalable, reliable systems: estimation, caching, databases, queues, consistency and the classic interview designs. Ends with frontend system design for full stack roles.

chapters.title: Requirements and Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
chapters.summary: How to open a system design interview: clarify requirements, then size the system with quick, defensible math.

lesson.heading: The shape of a system design interview
lesson.body:
A system design interview is a 45-60 minute conversation, not a quiz. The interviewer wants to see how you turn a vague prompt ('design Twitter') into a concrete, defensible architecture. A reliable structure:

- **Clarify requirements** (5 min): functional and non-functional.
- **Estimate scale** (5 min): users, QPS, storage, bandwidth.
- **Define the API and data model** (5-10 min).
- **High-level design** (10-15 min): boxes and arrows for the main flows.
- **Deep dive** (10-15 min): the hardest one or two components, bottlenecks, failure modes.
- **Wrap up**: trade-offs, what you would do next, monitoring.

Driving the conversation yourself, stating assumptions out loud and checking in with the interviewer matters as much as the final diagram.

lesson.heading: Functional vs non-functional requirements
lesson.body:
**Functional requirements** describe what the system does: 'users can post a tweet', 'users see a home timeline', 'short links redirect to the long URL'. Pick 3-5 core features and explicitly park the rest ('I will skip DMs and ads unless you want them').

**Non-functional requirements** describe how well it does it:

- Scale: daily active users (DAU), read/write ratio.
- Latency: for example p99 under 200 ms for reads.
- Availability: 99.9% is about 8.8 hours of downtime per year; 99.99% is about 53 minutes.
- Consistency: can users see stale data for a few seconds?
- Durability: can we ever lose data (payments: no; view counters: maybe).

Non-functional requirements drive almost every architectural choice. A read-heavy, eventually consistent feed looks nothing like a strongly consistent payment ledger.

lesson.heading: Numbers every engineer should know
lesson.body:
Estimation needs a few anchors. Approximate values:

- L1 cache reference: ~1 ns. Main memory reference: ~100 ns.
- Read 1 MB sequentially from memory: ~3-10 microseconds; from SSD: ~50-200 microseconds.
- Round trip within one data center: ~0.5 ms. Cross-continent round trip: ~70-150 ms.
- A single well-tuned Postgres or MySQL node: thousands to low tens of thousands of simple queries per second.
- A single Redis node: ~100k+ simple operations per second.
- 1 day is ~86,400 seconds; use **~100k seconds** for quick math.

Powers of two: 2^10 ~ 1 thousand (KB), 2^20 ~ 1 million (MB), 2^30 ~ 1 billion (GB), 2^40 ~ 1 trillion (TB). Precision is not the goal; being within an order of magnitude is.

lesson.heading: Estimating QPS, storage and bandwidth
lesson.body:
Work from users to requests:

- Average QPS = DAU x actions per user per day / 86,400.
- Peak QPS is usually 2-10x average (pick 2-3x unless traffic is spiky).
- Storage = new items per day x size per item x retention days (add replication factor, often 3x).
- Bandwidth = QPS x payload size.

Worked example: 100M DAU, each user writes 2 posts/day and reads 100 posts/day. Writes = 200M/day ~ 2,300/s average, ~5k/s peak. Reads = 10B/day ~ 115k/s average, ~300k/s peak. Read:write is 50:1, so caching and read replicas matter more than write throughput. If a post is 1 KB, storage is 200 GB/day, ~73 TB/year before replication.

State each assumption, round aggressively, and say what the number implies ('300k reads/s means we need a cache layer; one database will not serve that').

code.source:
DAU                = 100,000,000
writes/user/day    = 2      -> 200M writes/day
reads/user/day     = 100    -> 10B reads/day
seconds/day        ~ 100,000 (86,400)
write QPS (avg)    ~ 2,000   peak ~ 5,000
read QPS  (avg)    ~ 100,000 peak ~ 300,000
post size          = 1 KB   -> 200 GB/day -> ~73 TB/year (x3 replicas ~ 220 TB)

lesson.heading: Defining the API and data model early
lesson.body:
After sizing, sketch the API. It forces you to pin down what the system accepts and returns, and it reveals the access patterns that drive the data model.

- `POST /v1/posts {text, mediaIds}` returns `{postId}`
- `GET /v1/feed?cursor=...&limit=20` returns posts plus `nextCursor`

Then list the main entities and their key access patterns: 'get posts by user ordered by time', 'get followers of user'. Access patterns decide SQL vs NoSQL, indexes and partition keys. Prefer cursor-based pagination for feeds (stable under inserts) over offset pagination, which gets slow and skips or duplicates rows when data changes.

**Gotcha**: do not jump into technology names ('Kafka! Cassandra!') before requirements justify them. Interviewers penalise buzzword-driven designs.

keyPoints: Follow a structure: requirements, estimation, API, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs.
Functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional ones (scale, latency, availability, consistency) drive the architecture.
Use ~100k seconds per day for fast QPS math; peak is typically 2-10x average.
Storage = items/day x size x retention x replication factor.
The read:write ratio tells you whether to optimise reads (cache, replicas) or writes (partitioning, queues).
99.9% availability is ~8.8 h downtime/year; each extra nine is 10x less.
Define the API and access patterns before choosing databases.

questions.prompt: A service has 50M DAU and each user makes 20 requests per day. What is the approximate average QPS?
questions.explanation: 50M x 20 = 1B requests/day. 1B / 86,400 ~ 11,600, so roughly 12k QPS on average. Peak would be 2-3x that.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
options: Users can upload a profile photo
The home feed loads in under 200 ms at p99
questions.explanation: Latency targets describe how well the system performs, not what it does. The others are features (functional requirements).

questions.prompt: Roughly how much downtime per year does 99.99% availability allow?
questions.explanation: 0.01% of 525,600 minutes is ~52.6 minutes. 99.9% is ~8.8 hours and 99.999% is ~5 minutes.

questions.prompt: You store 10M new images per day, 500 KB each, kept for 5 years with 3x replication. Approximate raw storage?
questions.explanation: 10M x 500 KB = 5 TB/day. x 365 x 5 ~ 9.1 PB. x 3 replicas ~ 27 PB. Object storage with erasure coding would reduce the overhead, but the order of magnitude is petabytes.

questions.prompt: A system has a 100:1 read:write ratio. Which investment usually gives the biggest win?
options: A caching layer and read replicas
Switching to a message queue for writes
questions.explanation: When reads dominate, serving reads from cache or replicas offloads the primary. Write-path optimisations matter when writes are the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset pagination for a feed?
options: It stays stable when new items are inserted and avoids scanning skipped rows
It allows jumping to an arbitrary page number
It does not need an index
questions.explanation: Offset N forces the database to scan and discard N rows, and inserts shift pages, causing duplicates or gaps. A cursor (for example the last seen id or timestamp) seeks directly via an index.

questions.prompt: In an interview, you should produce exact capacity numbers to two significant figures before drawing any boxes.
questions.explanation: Estimates only need to be within an order of magnitude. Their purpose is to justify decisions (do we need a cache, sharding, a CDN), so round aggressively and move on.

questions.prompt: Peak QPS is commonly estimated as a small multiple (2-10x) of average QPS.
questions.explanation: Traffic follows daily cycles and events. Designing only for the average would cause overload at peak, so a multiplier is applied.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which questions belong in the requirements phase?
options: How many daily active users do we expect?
Which Kafka partitioner should we use?
Is it acceptable for a user to see slightly stale data?
Do we need to support editing posts?
Should the Redis eviction policy be allkeys-lru?
questions.explanation: Scale, consistency tolerance and feature scope are requirements. Kafka partitioners and Redis eviction policies are implementation details for the deep dive.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: for quick estimation, one day is about 86,400 ___ (round to 100k).
questions.explanation: 24 x 60 x 60 = 86,400 seconds. Rounding to 100k makes mental division easy.

questions.prompt: Estimate the storage and QPS for a photo-sharing app with 200M DAU where 10% of users upload 1 photo per day and everyone views 50 photos per day.
questions.answer:
- Uploads: 200M x 10% = 20M photos/day ~ 230/s average, ~700/s peak.
- Views: 200M x 50 = 10B/day ~ 115k/s average, ~350k/s peak. Read:write ~ 500:1.
- Size: assume 2 MB original plus ~300 KB of thumbnails, ~2.3 MB per photo -> ~46 TB/day, ~17 PB/year before replication.
- Bandwidth: if most views are 200 KB thumbnails, 115k/s x 200 KB ~ 23 GB/s egress, which clearly needs a CDN.
- Implications: blobs in object storage (S3-like), metadata in a database, CDN for serving, async processing pipeline for thumbnails, metadata reads behind a cache. I would state each assumption and confirm sizes with the interviewer.

questions.prompt: What questions do you ask in the first five minutes when given 'Design a chat application'?
questions.answer:
- Scope: 1:1 only or group chats? Max group size? Media messages? Read receipts, typing indicators, online presence?
- Platforms: mobile, web, both? Multi-device sync?
- Scale: DAU, messages per user per day, peak concurrent connections.
- Latency: what end-to-end delivery time is acceptable (for example under 500 ms)?
- Ordering and delivery guarantees: must messages be strictly ordered per conversation? At-least-once with dedupe?
- Retention: store history forever, or ephemeral? End-to-end encryption?
- Then I summarise the agreed scope ('1:1 and groups up to 500, text plus images, history stored, 100M DAU') before estimating.

questions.prompt: Why do non-functional requirements matter more than features in shaping an architecture? Give an example.
questions.answer: Features say which endpoints exist, but non-functional requirements decide how they are built. Two systems with identical features can need totally different designs. Example: a 'like' counter. If it must be exact and immediately consistent, every like is a transactional write to a primary database, which caps throughput. If a few seconds of staleness is fine, likes can be buffered in Redis or a queue and aggregated asynchronously, scaling to millions per second. Similarly, a 99.99% availability target forces multi-AZ redundancy and no single points of failure, while a 99% internal tool can run on one node. So I always pin down latency, availability, consistency and scale before drawing components.

chapters.title: Scalability and Load Balancing
chapters.summary: Vertical vs horizontal scaling, stateless services, and how load balancers spread traffic and survive failures.

lesson.heading: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
lesson.body:
**Vertical scaling** (scale up) means a bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disks. It is simple (no code changes, no distributed-systems problems) but has a hard ceiling, gets expensive non-linearly, and leaves a single point of failure.

**Horizontal scaling** (scale out) means more machines behind a load balancer. It has near-unlimited headroom and gives redundancy, but requires the application to be designed for it: no in-process session state, shared storage, and handling partial failures.

In practice teams scale vertically first for databases (it is cheap engineering time) and horizontally for stateless application servers from day one. Saying 'start with one big Postgres and read replicas, shard only when needed' is a mature answer.

lesson.heading: Stateless services
lesson.body:
A service is **stateless** when any instance can handle any request because no request depends on data held in a specific instance's memory or local disk. State moves to shared systems:

- Sessions in Redis or a signed JWT/cookie instead of server memory.
- Uploaded files in object storage (S3) instead of the local filesystem.
- Caches either shared (Redis) or treated as disposable local caches.

Stateless services can be added, removed or replaced at any time, which enables autoscaling, rolling deploys and recovery from crashed instances. **Sticky sessions** (the load balancer pins a user to one server) are a workaround for stateful apps, but they unbalance load and lose sessions when an instance dies.

lesson.heading: Load balancers: L4 vs L7
lesson.body:
A load balancer (LB) distributes requests across healthy backends.

- **Layer 4** (transport) balancers route TCP/UDP connections by IP and port without reading the payload. Very fast, protocol-agnostic. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer.
- **Layer 7** (application) balancers understand HTTP: they can route by path or host (`/api` to one pool, `/static` to another), terminate TLS, add headers, rewrite, and do retries. Examples: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode.

The LB itself must not be a single point of failure: managed cloud LBs are redundant internally; self-hosted ones run as an active-passive pair with a floating IP, or multiple instances behind DNS.

lesson.heading: Balancing algorithms and health checks
lesson.body:
Common algorithms:

- **Round robin**: next server in turn. Good when requests are uniform.
- **Weighted round robin**: bigger machines get more traffic.
- **Least connections / least outstanding requests**: better when request durations vary.
- **IP hash / consistent hashing**: the same client or key goes to the same backend, useful for cache affinity.
- **Power of two random choices**: pick two backends at random and send to the less loaded; near-optimal and cheap.

**Health checks** probe each backend (for example `GET /healthz` every 10 s). After N failures the backend is removed; after M successes it returns. Keep liveness checks shallow: if every instance's health check depends on the database, one database blip removes the whole fleet and turns a partial outage into a total one.

lesson.heading: Autoscaling and removing bottlenecks
lesson.body:
Horizontal scaling is usually paired with **autoscaling**: add instances when CPU, request count or queue depth crosses a threshold, remove them when it drops. Scale on a metric that reflects saturation (requests in flight, queue lag), and keep a warm minimum because new instances take time to boot.

Scaling the app tier only moves the bottleneck. Typical progression for a growing web app:

- One server -> separate database server.
- Add LB plus multiple stateless app servers.
- Add cache (Redis) and CDN for static assets.
- Add database read replicas.
- Move slow work to background queues.
- Shard or split the database by domain when writes outgrow one primary.

Always ask 'what breaks next at 10x?'

keyPoints: Vertical scaling is simple but capped and a single point of failure; horizontal scaling needs stateless design.
Move session, file and cache state out of app instances so any instance can serve any request.
L4 load balancers route connections; L7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by path, host or header.
Least-connections handles variable request times better than round robin.
Health checks remove failed backends; keep them shallow to avoid cascading removal.
The load balancer must be redundant itself.
Scaling one tier moves the bottleneck; plan the next one.

questions.prompt: Your app stores user sessions in server memory. After adding a second server behind a round-robin LB, users get logged out randomly. Best fix?
options: Store sessions in a shared store like Redis or use signed tokens
Switch to an L4 load balancer
questions.explanation: Requests land on a server that does not hold the session. Externalising session state makes the servers stateless. Sticky sessions hide the problem but break on instance failure and unbalance load.

questions.prompt: You need to route /api/* to one service and /images/* to another based on the URL path. Which load balancer type is required?
questions.explanation: Path-based routing requires parsing HTTP, which is a Layer 7 capability. L4 balancers only see IPs and ports.

questions.prompt: Requests to your service take anywhere from 5 ms to 5 s. Which algorithm spreads load most evenly?
questions.explanation: Round robin gives each server the same number of requests regardless of how long they run, so slow requests pile up. Least connections sends new work to the least busy server.

questions.prompt: Every app instance's /health endpoint queries the database. The database has a 30-second hiccup. What is the likely outcome?
options: Only the database is marked unhealthy
The LB removes all app instances, turning a partial outage into a full one
Nothing, health checks ignore database errors
Autoscaling adds more instances and fixes it
questions.explanation: Deep health checks couple instance health to a shared dependency. All instances fail together and the LB has nowhere to send traffic. Liveness checks should test the process itself; dependency status belongs in readiness or monitoring with care.

questions.prompt: Which is the main drawback of vertical scaling?
options: Hard upper limit and a single point of failure
questions.explanation: There is a biggest machine you can buy, and one machine fails as a unit. Vertical scaling needs no code changes, which is its advantage.

questions.prompt: Which metric is usually the best signal for autoscaling a worker fleet that consumes a queue?
questions.explanation: Queue lag directly measures whether consumers keep up with producers. CPU can be misleading for I/O-bound workers.

questions.prompt: A Layer 4 load balancer can terminate TLS and inspect HTTP headers to choose a backend.
questions.explanation: Header inspection requires Layer 7. An L4 balancer forwards TCP/UDP streams based on addresses and ports (some can pass TLS through or terminate it, but they do not route on HTTP content).

questions.prompt: Stateless application servers make rolling deployments and autoscaling easier.
questions.explanation: Since no instance holds unique state, instances can be started, drained and killed freely without losing user data.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: what makes a web service stateless-friendly?
options: Sessions in Redis or signed cookies
User uploads written to the instance's local disk
Files in object storage like S3
In-memory cache that is safe to lose
Background jobs tracked only in a process-local array
questions.explanation: Shared or disposable state is fine. Local-disk uploads and process-local job lists disappear or diverge when instances change.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: adding more machines behind a load balancer is called ___ scaling.
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds nodes; vertical scaling (scale up) makes one node bigger.

questions.prompt: Walk through how you would scale a monolithic web app from 1,000 to 10 million users.
questions.answer:
- Start: one server running app plus database. First split the database onto its own machine so they scale independently.
- Put a load balancer in front of 2+ stateless app servers; move sessions to Redis and files to S3. This also removes the app single point of failure.
- Add a CDN for static assets and a Redis cache for hot reads (cache-aside).
- Add database read replicas and route read-only queries to them; tolerate replication lag where acceptable.
- Move slow or bursty work (emails, image processing) to a queue with workers.
- Add autoscaling on request rate or latency, plus monitoring and alerting.
- When writes outgrow a single primary, partition: first by functional domain (separate databases per service), then shard hot tables by a key like user_id.
- Multi-AZ everywhere, and eventually multi-region if latency or availability targets demand it. At each step I measure first and fix the current bottleneck rather than prematurely distributing.

questions.prompt: How do you make a load balancer itself highly available?
questions.answer:
- Use a managed cloud LB (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP LB): it is internally redundant across availability zones and scales automatically.
- Self-hosted: run two or more LB nodes (HAProxy/Nginx/Envoy) in active-passive with a floating virtual IP managed by keepalived (VRRP), or active-active behind DNS with multiple A records or anycast.
- Spread LB nodes across availability zones.
- Health-check the LBs themselves and keep config in version control so a replacement is quick.
- For global traffic, use DNS-based or anycast global load balancing in front of regional LBs, so a whole region can fail over.

questions.prompt: When are sticky sessions acceptable, and what are their downsides?
questions.answer: Sticky sessions (session affinity) pin a client to one backend via a cookie or IP hash. They are acceptable as a temporary measure for legacy stateful apps, or when affinity improves performance (for example a WebSocket connection naturally stays on one server, or a per-node cache warms up for a user). Downsides: load becomes uneven (a few heavy users overload one node), scaling in or crashing an instance loses those users' in-memory sessions, deployments must drain carefully, and IP-hash breaks behind NATs where many users share one IP. The better long-term fix is externalising state so affinity becomes an optimisation rather than a correctness requirement.

chapters.title: Caching Layers and CDNs
chapters.summary: Where to cache, which caching pattern to use, how to invalidate, and how CDNs serve content close to users.

lesson.heading: Why and where to cache
lesson.body:
A cache stores the result of expensive work (a database query, a rendered page, an API call) in faster storage so repeated requests skip the work. Caches exist at every layer:

- **Browser cache**: controlled by `Cache-Control`, `ETag` headers.
- **CDN / edge cache**: static assets and cacheable HTML/API responses near users.
- **Reverse proxy cache**: Nginx or Varnish in front of the app.
- **Application cache**: Redis or Memcached shared by app servers, or an in-process LRU.
- **Database cache**: buffer pool, query cache, materialised views.

Caching works because access is skewed: a small fraction of keys (hot items) get most reads. The **hit ratio** is the key metric; a cache with a 50% hit ratio only halves database load, while 99% reduces it 100x.

lesson.heading: Caching patterns
lesson.body:
- **Cache-aside (lazy loading)**: the app reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache. Most common. Only requested data is cached, and a cache outage degrades to slower reads instead of failure.
- **Read-through**: the cache library itself loads from the database on a miss. Same idea, logic lives in the cache layer.
- **Write-through**: writes go to the cache and the database synchronously. Cache is always fresh, but writes are slower and unread data fills the cache.
- **Write-behind (write-back)**: writes go to the cache and are flushed to the database asynchronously. Very fast writes, but data can be lost if the cache dies before flushing.
- **Write-around**: writes go only to the database; the cache fills on reads. Good when written data is rarely re-read soon.

For most web apps: cache-aside for reads, and on writes update the database then **delete** the cache key (not update it), which avoids races where a stale value overwrites a newer one.

lesson.heading: Invalidation, TTLs and eviction
lesson.body:
'There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Strategies:

- **TTL**: every entry expires after N seconds. Bounds staleness, simple, always use one as a safety net.
- **Explicit invalidation**: delete keys when the source changes (on write, or via change-data-capture events).
- **Versioned keys**: include a version in the key (`product:42:v7`); bump the version to invalidate everything at once.

When memory is full the cache **evicts** entries: LRU (least recently used) is the common default; LFU (least frequently used) keeps long-term popular items; Redis offers policies like `allkeys-lru` and `volatile-ttl`. Add random jitter to TTLs so keys written together do not expire together.

lesson.heading: Cache failure modes
lesson.body:
- **Cache stampede (thundering herd)**: a hot key expires and thousands of requests miss simultaneously, all hitting the database. Fixes: a lock or single-flight so only one request recomputes, serve stale while revalidating, or refresh hot keys before expiry (probabilistic early expiration).
- **Cache penetration**: requests for keys that do not exist always miss and hit the database (often malicious). Fix: cache negative results briefly, or use a Bloom filter of valid keys.
- **Cache avalanche**: many keys expire at once, or the cache cluster restarts cold. Fix: TTL jitter, warm-up, and rate limiting to the database.
- **Hot key**: one key receives more traffic than a single cache node can serve. Fix: replicate the key across nodes (`key#1..key#N`) or add a small in-process cache in front.
- **Stale data / inconsistency**: write to DB succeeded but delete from cache failed. Fix: short TTLs, retries, or CDC-driven invalidation.

lesson.heading: CDNs and HTTP caching
lesson.body:
A **Content Delivery Network** (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai) is a set of edge servers (points of presence) worldwide. Users hit the nearest edge; on a miss the edge fetches from your **origin** and caches the response. Benefits: lower latency, offloaded origin bandwidth, DDoS absorption, TLS termination at the edge.

- **Pull CDN**: edge fetches from origin on first request. Simple, the default.
- **Push CDN**: you upload content to the CDN ahead of time. Useful for large files with predictable demand.

Caching behaviour is driven by HTTP headers. Fingerprinted assets (`app.3f9a1c.js`) can be cached forever with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, because a new deploy changes the file name. HTML should use short TTLs or `no-cache` with `ETag` revalidation. `s-maxage` sets the TTL for shared caches (CDN) separately from browsers, and `stale-while-revalidate` lets the edge serve stale content while refreshing in the background. Purge APIs invalidate content after urgent changes.

code.source:
# Hashed static asset: cache forever
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# HTML page: CDN caches 60 s, may serve stale up to 5 min while refreshing
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

# Private per-user API response: never store in shared caches
Cache-Control: private, no-store

keyPoints: Caching pays off because access is skewed; hit ratio is the key metric.
Cache-aside is the default: read cache, on miss load from DB and populate.
On writes, update the database then delete the cache key rather than writing the new value.
Always set TTLs (with jitter) as a safety net for staleness.
Guard against stampedes with single-flight locks or stale-while-revalidate.
CDNs cache content at edge locations near users and shield the origin.
Fingerprinted static assets can be cached for a year with immutable; HTML gets short TTLs.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, what happens on a cache miss?
options: The application reads from the database and writes the result into the cache
The cache itself queries the database transparently
The database pushes the value into the cache
questions.explanation: In cache-aside the application owns the logic. A cache that loads data itself on a miss is the read-through pattern.

questions.prompt: Which write strategy offers the fastest writes but risks data loss if the cache node crashes?
questions.explanation: Write-behind acknowledges the write once it is in the cache and flushes later; unflushed writes are lost on a crash.

questions.prompt: A celebrity profile key expires and 50,000 concurrent requests all miss and query the database. What is this called?
questions.explanation: A stampede is many simultaneous misses on the same key. Single-flight recomputation or serving stale data while one request refreshes prevents it.

questions.prompt: Attackers request random non-existent product IDs, bypassing the cache every time. Best mitigation?
options: Cache negative results briefly and/or use a Bloom filter of valid IDs
questions.explanation: This is cache penetration. Caching 'not found' for a short time or checking a Bloom filter stops misses from reaching the database.

questions.prompt: Which header is appropriate for a fingerprinted bundle like main.8c1f2a.js?
questions.explanation: The hash changes whenever content changes, so the URL is effectively versioned. It can be cached for a year and never revalidated.

questions.code:
await db.products.update(id, data);
await redis.set(`product:${id}`, JSON.stringify(data));
questions.prompt: Two concurrent updates run this code. What risk does setting (instead of deleting) the cache create?
options: None, it is the recommended pattern
Writes can interleave so the cache ends with the older value while the database has the newer one
questions.explanation: Request A writes DB, request B writes DB, B sets cache, then A sets cache: the cache now holds A's stale value indefinitely. Deleting the key forces the next read to load the current value.

questions.prompt: Adding random jitter to TTLs helps prevent many keys from expiring at the same moment.
questions.explanation: Keys populated together (for example after a deploy or warm-up) would otherwise expire together, causing a burst of misses (avalanche).

questions.prompt: A CDN is only useful for static files such as images and JavaScript.
questions.explanation: CDNs also cache HTML and public API responses, terminate TLS near users, absorb DDoS traffic and can run edge functions.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: valid ways to reduce cache stampedes on a hot key.
options: Single-flight lock so only one request recomputes the value
Serve stale data while refreshing in the background
Refresh the value proactively before expiry
Disable the cache during peak hours
questions.explanation: Locks, stale-while-revalidate and early refresh all ensure the database sees one recomputation instead of thousands. A zero TTL or disabling the cache makes it worse.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the most common cache eviction policy, which removes the entry not accessed for the longest time, is ___.
questions.explanation: LRU assumes recently used items are likely to be used again. LFU, FIFO and TTL-based policies are alternatives.

questions.prompt: Design the caching strategy for a product detail page on an e-commerce site with 50k reads/s and frequent price updates.
questions.answer:
- Split data by volatility: static content (title, images, description) changes rarely; price and stock change often.
- CDN: cache the page shell and images at the edge with s-maxage of a few minutes plus stale-while-revalidate; fetch price/stock client-side or via an edge include with a short TTL (or no cache).
- Application cache: Redis cache-aside for product data, key product:{id}, TTL with jitter (for example 10 min); price/stock keys with short TTL (10-30 s) or explicit invalidation.
- Invalidation: on price change, write DB then delete the Redis key and optionally purge the CDN path; a CDC stream (Debezium) from the DB can drive invalidation reliably.
- Stampede protection for hot products: single-flight recomputation and early refresh.
- Checkout must never trust cached price: re-read authoritative price and stock from the database inside the order transaction.
- Monitor hit ratio, p99 latency and DB QPS; alert if hit ratio drops.

questions.prompt: Explain the trade-offs between write-through, write-behind and cache-aside.
questions.answer:
- Cache-aside: app reads cache, loads DB on miss, deletes key on write. Pros: simple, caches only what is read, cache failure is non-fatal. Cons: first read is slow, small window of staleness, app code holds cache logic.
- Write-through: every write updates cache and DB synchronously. Pros: cache always fresh for written keys, reads after writes hit. Cons: higher write latency, caches data that may never be read, still needs TTL/eviction.
- Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously in batches. Pros: very low write latency, batching reduces DB load (good for counters, metrics). Cons: data loss risk on cache failure, complex ordering and consistency, DB lags.
- Choice: cache-aside for general reads; write-through when read-after-write must hit cache; write-behind only for loss-tolerant high-write data like view counts.

questions.prompt: How does a CDN decide whether to serve from cache or go to origin, and how do you deploy a new frontend version safely?
questions.answer:
- The edge computes a cache key (typically scheme, host, path, and configured query params/headers) and looks it up. If present and fresh per Cache-Control (s-maxage/max-age), it serves it; if stale it may revalidate with the origin using ETag/If-None-Match or serve stale under stale-while-revalidate; on miss it fetches from origin (possibly via a regional shield tier) and stores the response if cacheable.
- Safe deploy: build assets with content hashes in file names and upload them first with a one-year immutable TTL. Then deploy the HTML (short TTL or no-cache) that references the new hashes. Old HTML still points at old assets, which remain available, so no user gets a mismatched bundle.
- Keep old assets for a while for clients with cached HTML, and purge only the HTML paths if needed.

chapters.title: Database Scaling: Replication, Partitioning and Sharding
chapters.summary: How databases grow past one node: read replicas, leader election, partitioning schemes, consistent hashing and the costs of sharding.

lesson.heading: Choosing a data store
lesson.body:
Start from access patterns, not fashion.

- **Relational (Postgres, MySQL)**: joins, transactions, constraints, flexible queries. The right default for most business data.
- **Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB)**: lookups by key at huge scale with predictable latency.
- **Wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB)**: very high write throughput, queries designed around a partition key, tunable consistency.
- **Document (MongoDB)**: nested JSON documents read as a whole.
- **Search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch)**: full-text and faceted search, usually fed from a primary store.
- **Object storage (S3)**: large blobs; keep metadata in a database.

Many systems are **polyglot**: Postgres as source of truth, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search, S3 for media. Every additional store adds a synchronisation problem, so justify each one.

lesson.heading: Replication
lesson.body:
Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes for availability and read scaling.

- **Leader-follower (primary-replica)**: all writes go to the leader, which streams its log to followers. Reads can go to followers. Used by Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB replica sets.
- **Synchronous** replication waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging the write: no data loss on leader failure, but higher latency and writes block if the follower is down. **Asynchronous** is faster but can lose the last few writes on failover. A common compromise is one synchronous plus several async followers (semi-sync).
- **Multi-leader**: several nodes accept writes (for example one per region). Needs conflict resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs, app logic).
- **Leaderless** (Dynamo-style, Cassandra): clients write to and read from several replicas; with N replicas, W write acks and R read responses, **R + W > N** guarantees the read set overlaps the latest write.

**Replication lag** causes anomalies: a user updates their profile then reloads from a lagging replica and sees the old value. Fix with **read-your-writes** routing (read from the leader for a few seconds after a user writes, or track the log position).

lesson.heading: Failover
lesson.body:
When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted. Steps: detect failure (heartbeats with timeouts), elect the most up-to-date follower (via a consensus system like etcd/ZooKeeper, or a managed service such as RDS Multi-AZ or Patroni for Postgres), and redirect clients (DNS or proxy update).

Risks:

- **Data loss** with async replication: the new leader may miss writes the old one acknowledged.
- **Split brain**: the old leader comes back and still thinks it is leader; two nodes accept writes. Prevented with fencing tokens or STONITH (shoot the other node in the head).
- **Timeout tuning**: too short causes unnecessary failovers under load; too long extends outages.

lesson.heading: Partitioning and sharding
lesson.body:
**Partitioning** splits a dataset into pieces. **Vertical partitioning** splits by columns or by feature (users DB, orders DB). **Horizontal partitioning** splits rows; when the pieces live on different servers it is called **sharding**.

Sharding strategies:

- **Range-based**: `user_id 1-1M` on shard A, and so on. Efficient range scans, but sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment ids) create hot shards.
- **Hash-based**: `shard = hash(key) % N`. Even distribution, but range queries hit all shards, and changing N remaps almost every key.
- **Directory/lookup-based**: a lookup service maps key to shard. Flexible, but the directory is an extra dependency.
- **Consistent hashing**: keys and nodes are placed on a hash ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node moves only ~1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth the distribution.

Choosing the **shard key** is the critical decision: it should have high cardinality, spread load evenly and keep the most common queries on a single shard (for example `tenant_id` for a SaaS app, `conversation_id` for messages).

lesson.heading: The cost of sharding
lesson.body:
Sharding solves write and storage limits but adds real complexity:

- **Cross-shard queries and joins** become scatter-gather or must be denormalised.
- **Cross-shard transactions** need two-phase commit or sagas; most designs avoid them by choosing a shard key that keeps a transaction local.
- **Rebalancing** data when adding shards must happen online without downtime.
- **Hot spots**: a celebrity user or large tenant can overload one shard; split hot keys or give big tenants dedicated shards.
- **Global unique IDs**: auto-increment no longer works; use UUIDv7, ULIDs or Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + machine id + sequence) which are also roughly time-sortable.

Before sharding, exhaust cheaper options: indexes and query tuning, caching, read replicas, archiving old data, vertical scaling, and table partitioning within one node (Postgres declarative partitioning). Managed distributed SQL (CockroachDB, Spanner, Vitess for MySQL, Citus for Postgres) can shard for you.

keyPoints: Pick data stores by access pattern; relational is the default for business data.
Leader-follower replication scales reads; async replication risks losing recent writes on failover.
Replication lag breaks read-your-writes; route a user's reads to the leader after they write.
In leaderless systems, R + W > N gives overlapping quorums.
Sharding splits rows across nodes; the shard key decides balance and query locality.
hash % N remaps most keys when N changes; consistent hashing moves only ~1/N.
Prevent split brain with consensus-based election and fencing.
Exhaust indexing, caching, replicas and vertical scaling before sharding.

questions.prompt: A user edits their bio, the page reloads, and the old bio appears for a few seconds. Most likely cause?
options: Reading from an asynchronously replicated follower that lags the leader
questions.explanation: The write went to the leader but the read hit a replica that had not applied it yet. Read-your-writes routing fixes it.

questions.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store with N = 3 replicas, which setting guarantees reads see the latest acknowledged write?
questions.explanation: R + W must exceed N so the read and write sets overlap. 2 + 2 = 4 > 3. All other options sum to 3 or less.

questions.prompt: You shard with shard = hash(userId) % 8 and grow to 9 shards. Roughly what fraction of keys must move?
questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing N changes the result for almost every key (about N/(N+1) of them). Consistent hashing would move only ~1/9.

questions.prompt: Range-sharding an events table by created_at timestamp causes which problem?
options: All new writes land on the newest shard, creating a hot spot
questions.explanation: Monotonic keys send every insert to the last range. Hashing the key or prefixing with a hashed bucket spreads writes.

questions.prompt: For a multi-tenant SaaS app where nearly every query filters by tenant, which shard key is usually best?
questions.explanation: tenant_id keeps each tenant's queries and transactions on one shard. Random UUIDs balance load but force scatter-gather queries; country has low cardinality and skew.

questions.prompt: What problem do fencing tokens solve during failover?
options: A former leader continuing to accept writes after a new leader is elected (split brain)
questions.explanation: Each new leader gets a higher token; storage rejects writes carrying an older token, so a zombie leader cannot corrupt data.

questions.prompt: Synchronous replication to at least one follower prevents losing acknowledged writes when the leader fails.
questions.explanation: The write is only acknowledged once a follower has it, so that follower can be promoted without loss. The cost is higher write latency.

questions.prompt: Auto-increment primary keys work unchanged across independently sharded databases.
questions.explanation: Each shard would generate the same ids. Use UUIDv7, ULIDs, Snowflake-style ids or a central id allocator.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: things to try before sharding a relational database.
options: Add missing indexes and fix slow queries
Rewrite the app in a new language
questions.explanation: Indexes, replicas, caches and archiving relieve most load cheaply. Language choice rarely limits database throughput.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: placing nodes and keys on a hash ring so that adding a node moves only ~1/N of keys is called ___ hashing.
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing (used by Dynamo, Cassandra, many caches) limits data movement when the cluster changes size.

questions.prompt: Your Postgres primary is at 80% CPU from reads and writes are growing 10% a month. Walk through your scaling plan.
questions.answer:
- Measure first: pg_stat_statements to find top queries by total time; add or fix indexes, remove N+1 queries. This alone often halves load.
- Offload reads: Redis cache-aside for hot reads, then read replicas with read-your-writes routing for user-facing paths. Use a connection pooler (PgBouncer) since Postgres connections are expensive.
- Reduce write cost: batch writes, move non-critical writes (analytics, audit) to a queue or separate store, archive cold rows, use table partitioning for large time-series tables.
- Scale up the primary if headroom is cheap, it buys months.
- If writes still outgrow one node: split by domain first (separate databases per bounded context), then shard the hottest domain by a key that keeps transactions local (tenant_id/user_id), or adopt Citus/managed distributed SQL.
- Throughout: monitor replication lag, CPU, IOPS, connection count, and set a capacity forecast so we act before hitting limits.

questions.prompt: Explain consistent hashing and why virtual nodes are used.
questions.answer: Consistent hashing maps both nodes and keys onto the same circular hash space (for example 0 to 2^32-1). A key is owned by the first node found moving clockwise from the key's hash. When a node joins, it takes over only the keys between itself and its predecessor; when one leaves, only its keys move to the successor. So about 1/N of keys move instead of nearly all with modulo hashing. With few physical nodes, random positions produce uneven arcs, so some nodes own much more data. Virtual nodes place each physical server at many points (for example 100-256) on the ring, which evens out load, spreads a failed node's keys across many survivors instead of one neighbour, and lets bigger machines take more vnodes. Replication is often done by storing a key on the next R distinct physical nodes clockwise.

questions.prompt: How would you generate globally unique, roughly time-ordered IDs across 1,000 shards without coordination on every insert?
questions.answer:
- Snowflake-style 64-bit ID: 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (~69 years), 10 bits of worker/machine id (1,024 workers), 12 bits of per-millisecond sequence (4,096 ids per ms per worker).
- Worker ids are assigned once at startup from a coordinator (ZooKeeper/etcd lease or config), so no per-insert coordination.
- IDs sort roughly by time, which keeps B-tree index inserts mostly append-only and enables time-based cursors.
- Handle clock skew: refuse to generate (or wait) if the clock moves backwards.
- Alternatives: UUIDv7 (128-bit, time-ordered, no worker assignment needed, larger) or ULID. Random UUIDv4 avoids coordination but fragments indexes and is not sortable.

questions.prompt: Compare leader-follower, multi-leader and leaderless replication. When would you pick each?
questions.answer:
- Leader-follower: one writer, simple consistency, easy reasoning, replicas for reads and failover. Default for relational databases and most apps. Limits: write throughput of one node and failover gaps.
- Multi-leader: each region (or device) accepts writes locally and syncs asynchronously. Good for multi-region active-active with low write latency, offline-first apps, collaborative editing. Cost: write conflicts that need last-write-wins, CRDTs or custom merge logic.
- Leaderless (Dynamo/Cassandra): any replica accepts writes, quorums (R + W > N) tune consistency, read repair and hinted handoff heal divergence. Good for very high write availability and throughput where eventual consistency is acceptable (event logs, IoT, user activity). Cost: no transactions across keys, conflict handling, careful data modelling around partition keys.
